speechtext:
I wish to put a question to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier).
Two lives having been lost recently as a result of the collapse of part of the ice bridge between Cross Point, Quebec, and Campbellton, New Brunswick, I would like the hon. Minister of Public Works to tell me:
1.	Whether he has received from the government of the province of Quebec or from that of New Brunswick any representations through which these provinces have formally agreed to participate financially in the construction of an interprovincial bridge between Cross Point and Campbellton.
2.	Whether the federal government is willing to participate financially in the construction of such an interprovincial bridge, according to the practice generally adopted up to now in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO BRIDGE BETWEEN CROSS POINT, P.Q. AND CAMPBELLTON, N.B.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of the construction of an interprovincial bridge between Cross Point and Campbellton has been brought time and again to the atten-

tion of my department by those members representing the neighbouring constituencies, including the one who asked this question.
Each time, I pointed out to hon. members that the federal government is always prepared to consider any proper suggestion that the two provincial governments might submit. However, no suggestion of the kind has yet been submitted to us by the provincial authorities concerned, neither jointly nor separately.
I should like to add that as soon as the two provinces concerned have formally indicated their decision to participate financially in the construction of this interprovincial bridge, I shall submit their proposals without delay to my colleagues of the cabinet.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate is now going into its second week. During that time the Department of National Defence has acquired an unenviable reputation. It has become a joke and the laughingstock of this country. Worse than that, the present administration of the department has brought the department itself, and particularly the army branch, to a position where it also has become a laughingstock in the country. That, I suggest, is a very regrettable affair. The Department of National Defence is not only the largest spending department of the government but it is the department that is concerned with the nation's very survival in time of war. It is the department which is concerned not only with the spending of hundreds of millions of dollars but the department which is concerned with the life and welfare of thousands of our citizens who enlist in the various branches of the services. It is the department that must inspire young Canadians with sufficient confidence to induce large numbers of them to choose the armed services as their lifework and to inspire still larger numbers to submit themselves to sufficient training to enable us to defend ourselves in case of attack.
It is not good for the morale of the army or the morale of the Department of National Defence, nor is it good for the morale of the
Committee on Defence Expenditure country, that a department of such importance should become the laughingstock of the country, particularly at this time. When have we ever before in all the history of Canada had a department of national defence that has become, as this administration has, the subject of such numerous jokes by joke-sters and cartoonists all across the country? When has any one of our great national dailies ever had the opportunity of making such fun at the expense of the Department of National Defence as the Globe and Mail did on the front page of its issue of January 15? I have a copy of that page on my desk. There is a whole page of cartoons gathered from all across the country that hold the Department of National Defence up to ridicule.
There is a cartoon, for instance, representing an ordinary soldier up before the big brass of the army and defending himself by saying, "All I said was, I have been working like a horse." The present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), Mr. Speaker, is the most nagged man in all Canada today.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is only your opinion.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is small wonder that the Department of National Defence has become an object of such ridicule. When before in our history has Hansard ever printed on one day a letter tabled by a minister of a responsible department, a letter supposed to be written by him, signed by him and sent by him to another citizen, only to be told on the next day by the minister that he did not write the letter, he did not dictate it and the signature must have been added at some stage either by a clerk or by a printer? It becomes quite evident to the public that the minister is not only unfamiliar with what goes on in his own department but he does not even know what he is doing when he is tabling documents in the House of Commons. He does not even know what he is tabling. How can we expect the country to have confidence in an administration of that kind? What goes on in the Department of National Defence? Who played such a prank on the minister? I suggest that this is a case worthy of the best efforts of the R.C.M.P. Certainly it is as worthy as some of the duties that have been assigned to that force by the Department of Justice in recent weeks.
The debate, as I said, has gone on now for two weeks. During that time the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) have all participated along with some other lesser Liberal lights. Actually the big Klieg lights of the Liberal party and the little candle lights, as for example, the
1222	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure one from Mackenzie, have only served to blur the picture before us. What has quite evidently been the object of the government in this debate is the minimizing of the importance of the actual report and drawing the attention of the public to other minor and side issues.
I submit it is in the public interest that our attention should be focused on the report and the revelation of inefficiency on the part of those at or near the top of the Department of National Defence as exposed in the report. That is the issue which should be our concern. It is not, I submit, a matter of grave national importance whether a colonel's rocking horse was a $400 bang-up thoroughbred affair with a silken mane, as the soldier who made it evidently thought, or whether it was, as the minister says, a rough affair made from scrap, from a lady's worn-out fur coat and a milkman's horse's tail, a rocking horse that was only worth $9.50-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Your party brought it up.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-and which $9.50 was returned to the government some weeks or months after the horse was made and after the investigation was well under way. It is a matter of some importance that an investigation by an investigator of Mr. Currie's standing gives us certain important facts. It is important that the explanations that the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister have given us pertaining to the same facts are at variance with and contradictory to those given by Mr. Currie. This becomes more important when we are given to understand by the minister that Mr. Currie got his information from the Department of National Defence, that the department cooperated with him in giving him all the information he wanted, and that the reason the minister wanted the Department of National Defence to check the report was that the facts had been given by the department.
The minister and the Prime Minister got their facts from the Department of National Defence. Yet they are at variance in a number of details. How does it happen, for instance, that Mr. Currie's story about horses on the payroll should differ so widely from the Prime Minister's explanation? How does it come about ,that Mr. Currie could find no useful purpose being served by a certain dam that was built and yet the Minister of National Defence comes forward with an explanation? How does it happen that nobody in the Department of National Defence was bright enough to think of these explanations when Mr. Currie interrogated them and that the explanations come to us only after


Mr. Currie has given us an entirely different version? Any impartial citizen who is at all interested in this affair can only reach one conclusion. That one and only conclusion is that the government is going to great lengths to whitewash the Currie report.
It is a matter of some public concern, I think, whether a government department being investigated should have the right to edit a report which exposes the inefficiency of the department being investigated. Is it the right of the Department of National Defence to have that report, which condemns that department for its inefficiency, revised and edited by that department before it is made public? That, I take it, is a question of some national importance.
The minister tries to gloss over that fact, without really facing up to it, by telling us that he ordered the report; that he wanted the truth; and apparently he admits that Mr. Currie could not get at the truth and so the minister has to get at it after the report is published. He tells us that Mr. Currie got his information from the department but the department wanted to check the facts that it gave to Mr. Currie.
The whole question at issue is whether or not a government department that is being investigated can require the submission to it of a report of the investigation which condemns that department for inefficiency- before the report is made public. You do not answer that question by saying that this report was Mr. Currie's; that Mr. Currie could submit it or not as he chose; that Mr. Currie could take the suggestion of the Department of National Defence or not as he pleased. That does not answer the question.
We shall never know what conversations took place nor what persuasive measures were taken to induce Mr. Currie to comply with the minister's request in this respect. I say that it was submitted for editing advisedly, because in my opinion the change that was made in that report, changing the wording from "those at or near the top" to read "higher ups" cannot by any stretch of the imagination be considered factual or anything else but editing. That was the real purpose why that report had to be submitted to the officers of the Department of National Defence.
Let us not forget that had it not been for the fact that what the Prime Minister calls a preliminary working paper found its way into the hands of the leader of this group, the country would never have known that Mr. Currie was requested by the Department of National Defence to submit his report to them for editing before it was tabled in this house.

Some of us believe that a department of government being investigated should not be accorded the privilege of editing a report made by an independent investigator condemning that department. We believe that a report produced and made public under those restrictive conditions could-I am not saying that this one did-lose all of its validity as an independent report by an independent investigator. On those grounds we think that the department should not have been accorded that privilege. In fact, some of us feel so strongly on this point that we believe that the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) would have been condoning the action of the government and would not have been fulfilling his duty as a member of this house if he had, as the Prime Minister suggested, refused to make use of the information which came into his hands.
Are we to assume that only the government has the right to make use of stolen information-if it was stolen? No one questioned the right of the government to make use of stolen information in the Russian spy case. Are we to accord that right only to the government or, as the Prime Minister suggested, to the leader of the official opposition? As he suggested, had the report been taken to the editors of the country-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who stole the report?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-it might have been taken to the leader of the official opposition. Are we to accord that privilege to those people and not accord it to the opposition members of parliament? That is an issue, I think, which might well be considered.
The Prime Minister on January 15, when speaking in this house about the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), as reported in Hansard on page 1019, said: -the hon. gentleman is sometimes inclined to set himself up not only as an authority, . . . but also as an example of rectitude for the rest of us to follow in our own public conduct.
Then a few minutes later the Prime Minister, as reported on page 1021, sets himself up as an example to the rest of us when he makes this statement:
Does anyone imagine, Mr. Speaker, that I would be doing lor anyone but the public service what I have been doing for the last four or five years for the pecuniary compensation that I get for it?
I am not for one moment questioning the fact that the Prime Minister was rendering this service because of his interest in the public and in the welfare of Canada, but what I am saying is that the Prime Minister should be broad-minded enough to accord to gentlemen on this side of the house the same privileges that he takes unto himself and that he takes for the members of his government.
Committee on Defence Expenditure

speechtext: He did not steal anything.

speechtext: Is the Prime Minister unwilling to concede that the member for Rosetown-Biggar used that information for no other purpose than in the public interest? He implies in his speech that the man who brought that information to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: -was not only stealing this information but that he was bringing the document solely for the purpose of its being used in party strife. The Prime Minister insinuated that the member for Rosetown-Biggar, when he made use of that information, was making use of it for no other purpose than party strife. Is the Prime Minister not big enough, is he not gentlemanly enough, to assume that there could be some people on this side of the house whose principles are high enough-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to know if the word "insinuate", in this case, is unparliamentary?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Look it up in the dictionary.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let the Speaker decide. To me the word "insinuate" means lied. I should like to know whether or not, in the present circumstances, that word is unparliamentary. I am waiting for your decision, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not think I should rule that the word "insinuate" is out of order. I do not think it means "to lie". Many things may be insinuated. I cannot declare it to be unparliamentary in the present circumstances.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Nor could anyone else.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
By what means does the Prime Minister arrive at his conclusion that because opposition members cannot identify the interests of the Liberal party with the interests of the country, as quite evidently the Liberals do, they are therefore stooping to party strife? They have attempted to expose a government practice which they consider wrong, and which they consider against the public interest. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, we in this group believe that the exposure of the government's insistence on editing the Currie report is not in the best interests of Canada, and that those who exposed that were, in reality, rendering the country a good public service.
Apart altogether from the question of the document and the issue arising out of it, I want to support the subamendment moved by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. 1224	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure Knowles). The subamendment, on page 1019 of Hansard for January 15, 1953, reads in part as follows:
-and to give consideration to the desirability of recommending that Mr. Currie be asked to conduct a further inquiry into any other expenditures and commitments covered by the terms of this resolution.
If the Currie report has done nothing else, it has alerted the public to the fact that they are not getting value for all the money the Department of National Defence is spending. The public not only regard the administration of that department, as I said before, as a joke, but they have become cynical about it. They have become suspicious of what is happening elsewhere in that department. In my opinion, public interest and the interests of the Department of National Defence require that there be a thoroughgoing investigation of the expenditures of that whole department. Only in that way will public confidence in the department be restored to the point where the public will be willing to see *our youths devote their services to this country through the Department of National Defence.
Today this department is completely discredited in the eyes of the public, and only such a thoroughgoing investigation can restore that department to the confidence of the public. The minister tells us that he wants to get at the truth. I am confident the Prime Minister also wants to get at the truth. Yet, both of them will oppose this subamendment. The Prime Minister has told us he will vote against it, and he thereby gives the signal to all his followers to vote against it. Why? Certainly, they cannot pretend to those of us who sit in this house that they believe for one moment the committee on defence expenditure will make any such investigation of the true facts? They will get from that committee just those facts that the government wants revealed, and nothing more. Those of us who have had experience in sitting on committees in the past, and I sat on the defence expenditure committee during world war II, realize that they get just what information the government wants them to get.
I believe the keynote of the committee's investigation was given in an interview by Mr. MacTavish, president of the national Liberal federation, as reported in yesterday's Journal. Mr. MacTavish was interviewed during his first western trip in his present capacity, and had this to say:
-he believes the report will be put in its proper perspective after it is examined and analysed by the defence expenditures committee of the Commons.


Then he goes on to say that it will not be an issue in the forthcoming election. The report will be put in its proper perspective by the Liberal majority of that committee. They will minimize the charges in the report, and give the report such a good coat of whitewash that the Liberals hope the country will forget the report when election time comes, thus exonerating the government and the Department of National Defence from the charges that are implicit in that report. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the good name of our Department of National Defence, the good name and reputation of our armed forces acquired through the sacrifices of our soldiers, sailors and airmen in two world wars, is being sacrificed and held up to ridicule in this country because the Liberal party places party interests before national interest.
If the government today uses its majority in this house to defeat that subamendment, and thereby show the country that they do not want a thorough investigation into the Department of National Defence, they will furnish the country with proof of what I have just said.

speechtext:
I have been reluctant to enter the debate on the establishment of a committee to investigate defence expenditures and examine the Currie report. Rumour has it that I shall have ample opportunity in the very near future of discussing the Currie report. The house will understand, therefore, if I do not discuss it at the present time. But in listening to the debate, and I have listened to it since its inception, I have had a curious feeling of unreality. Let us see what the government is proposing to this house. The government is proposing, and I quote:
That a select committee be appointed to continue the examination of all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since March 31, 1950, and initially to give priority in their examination to the expenditures and commitments of the Canadian army works services as dealt with in the report of G. S. Currie, Esquire, chartered accountant, tabled in the House of Commons on December 15, 1952.
That is the government proposal. The position of the official opposition on that matter is well known and was stated by a member of last year's committee on Tuesday, January 20. As reported at page 1182 of Hansard of that day the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) said:
The idea of referring the report to the defence expenditure committee, from the point of view of the recommendations, is completely hopeless and just does not make sense.

Then again at page 1184:
I can think of nothing less valuable than to have the committee on defence expenditure spend its time, in effect, in investigating the investigator. That is what we would be doing, and that is all the defence expenditure committee can and will do if it is turned loose on this Currie report. We shall be investigating the investigator, the very man the Minister of National Defence and this government appointed for the purpose of investigating the irregularities which had taken place at Petawawa, who spent months in doing that, and who turned in what I think everyone will admit was an absolutely splendid report.
Then again at page 1186, still quoting the hon. member for Calgary East:
If this program envisaged by the government is carried out time will be spent on a minute examination and re-examination of the Currie report, and it will be a complete waste of time as far as the committee is concerned.
Then quoting the hon. member at page 1184 of Hansard:
Last year in the defence expenditure committee I made a motion that the committee should investigate the situation which had developed at Petawawa, but the government would not hear of it.
At that stage the hon. member for Calgary East neglected or in any event omitted the meat of his motion. The motion, as he states it, is tasteless, without being spiced. I cannot resist taking advantage of the opportunity to set the record clear.
On Tuesday, April 29, 1952, the committee on defence expenditure met and there were present Messrs. Adamson, Applewhaite, Blanchette, Campney, Cavers, Churchill, Croll, Dickey, Dinsdale-he had replaced the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) in that and a few other meetings; the hon. member for Nanaimo was away at that particular time -Fulton, Gauthier (Portneuf), George, Hark-ness, Henderson, James, Jones, Larson, Mac-donnell (Greenwood), Power, Stick and Weaver. Twenty-one members were present. Six members belonged to the official opposition; they were all present.
At that time the hon. member for Calgary East introduced a motion before that committee. I think I can tell you now that all the members of the official opposition voted for the motion of the hon. member for Calgary East and gave rather emphatic speeches on behalf of it. Let me read you the motion, Mr. Speaker; this is his notice of motion. It has four parts, (a), (b), (c) and (d) and it reads as follows:
(a)	That the Department of National Defence be asked to bring before the committee at its next meeting officials who can give us the general administrative set-up at Petawawa.
(b)	That witnesses be called before the committee to outline the losses of stores, etc., which have taken place at Petawawa, and the manner in which these losses occurred.
Committee on Defence Expenditure
(c)	That witnesses be called to outline the accounting and other procedures in use at Petawawa and other places to prevent loss and waste of government property.
Before I read (d) to you, Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat the proposal of the government before this house at the present time, namely:
That a select committee be appointed to continue the examination of all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since March 31, 1950, and initially to give priority in their examination to the expenditures and commitments of the Canadian army works services as dealt with in the report of G. S. Currie, Esquire, chartered accountant, tabled in the House of Commons on December 15, 1952.
I now read section (d) of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Calgary East and supported by all the members of the opposition whose names I have read, all of whom have spoken in this house and all of whom support his point of view. It reads:
(d)	That as soon as Mr. George S. Currie has completed his investigation at Petawawa, his report be placed before this committee and that he be called for questioning on it.

Mr. Speaker, from both the Currie report and the Sellar report one thing is clear to me, and that is that the biggest business operation being conducted in this country today, namely the Department of National Defence, is being conducted on sloppy, inefficient and unbusinesslike lines. Both these reports have pointed out that little heed has been paid to accounting methods and accounting; and after all, accounting is the backbone of any successful business operation.
When he was speaking on Tuesday night, the minister made a rather startling admission. He admitted that he had not read any of the 1,185 auditors' reports dealing with conditions in his department, and that he was therefore unfamiliar with what those reports contained.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

Then I think that makes it doubly shocking, Mr. Speaker, that someone in charge of a business operation which spends over $2 billion of the taxpayers' money each year, and which spends fifty cents out of every tax dollar collected from the Canadian people, has never bothered to look at an auditor's report on the conditions existing in his department. To me that is an exceedingly startling revelation.
When he was speaking in this house on Tuesday night, the minister said that not one member of the opposition had offered a constructive suggestion as to how the irregularities
1226	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure mentioned in Mr. Currie's report could have been prevented. I say to the minister that if he had paid some attention to the continuous reports of the chief auditor in his department, there would have been no necessity for Mr. Currie to make his investigation, because the conditions which necessitated that investigation would have been stamped out several years before.
If the president and the board of directors of a business corporation tried to defend this kind of negligence to the shareholders, all of them would be fired at the next annual meeting. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the cabinet are the president and board of directors of this country. They have taken the position that they have nothing to excuse with regard to the administration of the defence department. They are, in so many words, condoning these irregularities brought to light by Mr. Currie, and, in so doing, are saying to all other departments, "Do not be too careful about wasting the taxpayers' money. Go ahead and waste a little, if you want to. We will not remonstrate with you."

The government is saying,
"There is lots more money where this came from. If you are a little short, we will take more from the taxpayers for you; because in the last six years we have been overtaxing the people of Canada by more than a million dollars a day in excess of what was needed to meet all requirements, and we cannot see any reason for stopping now."
And now, to show you how little the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and others in charge of the defence department know about its operations, I would like to compare two statements made recently by the minister and his associate minister.
Speaking on this matter on December 17 the Acting Minister of National Defence, as reported at page 864 of Hansard, told us that the army works services consisted of 7,500 personnel. When speaking in the house on January 13 the Minister of National Defence, dealing with the army works services, said, as reported at page 937 of Hansard, that the army works services was made up of 765 service personnel and 3,334 civilian personnel, for a total of 4,100. There is a difference of 3,400 between those two figures, or the equivalent of an army brigade.
What I want to know is this: What happened to that army brigade in three weeks' time? It was there on December 17, but it had disappeared by January 13. If the two ministers in charge of the department can, between them, lose an army brigade in three weeks, how in the world can they expect


those who are working for them to keep track of smaller items such as railway sidings, trainloads of cement, and all the other examples of unchecked waste of the taxpayers' money which was brought to light by the Currie report?

I believe this kind of inefficiency and lack of knowledge of what is going on by way of waste and extravagance in the department is just not good enough, as a national effort, to back up our young fighting men in Korea and northwestern Europe. Those young men are giving up their very best; and I believe they are deserving of the best from the department that is responsible for our whole defence effort.
There is nothing that saps the morale of fighting men quicker than the knowledge that there is inefficiency in high places; and the inefficiency in this case stems right from this government.
As a member of the reserve army between 1947 and 1951, and as one who attended Petawawa Camp in three of those four summers, * I want to say that I believe the personnel in both our active and reserve forces is absolutely first-class. I feel that it is no responsibility of those fine young men and women in our armed services that the conditions brought to light by Mr. Currie existed. The responsibility lies "at or near the top" of this defence department. They, together with the whole of the government, must share the responsibility for the fact that these conditions were allowed to exist for several years, despite the fact that the auditor of the department reported such conditions on several occasions.

By ignoring proper accounting methods, and the continued warnings of the auditors within the department, I believe the Minister of National Defence, and those associated with him in running the department, threw the door wide open for wrongdoers. To me, the great wonder is, as Mr. Currie said, that far more crooks did not walk through that door than actually did walk through it. Surely it is a great credit to the young men and women of our armed services that there was not far more pilfering and dishonesty than actually developed.
The other afternoon we were entertained by the presentation of the sequel to the Currie report-the Murray report-given to us by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray). He outlined the kind of irregularities which took place in connection with the construction of the Alaska highway during the period of the last war. According to him, what went on at Petawawa was simply child's play when compared with what went on in the construction of the Alaska highway.
All the hon. member for Cariboo succeeded in doing was to prove that this kind of waste and inefficiency in our defence department has been going on for at least ten years and, as in the present instance, the responsibility for that waste, mishandling and maladministration must be placed right on the shoulders of the government.
The people of Canada do not object to paying for the cost of defence if they feel that they are receiving value for their tax dollars.

If the people of Canada are to continue willingly to meet the huge cost of defence, then they must be assured that this kind of waste and extravagance does not exist in all other branches of the Department of National Defence.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house long. At the outset I must congratulate the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) on pinpointing exactly what the opposition wanted to have done some time ago. It seems to me that the man who was put in charge of digging into matters at Petawawa and who accused certain people of looting should have been able to keep track of his own papers and not allow someone to steal them. I do not think he can condemn too much what was done at Petawawa when he could not keep track of what he was doing himself.
I have no brief or sympathy for any man in the armed forces who swears allegiance to his Queen and country and then loots and pilfers at the expense of the Canadian people. The government has dealt with these matters when they have been brought to their attention and it has been pointed out that twelve of these men are now in penitentiary.
Every business in Canada allows for certain losses occurring, but in the armed forces it is a different matter. When a man swears allegiance to his Queen and country he should live up to his signature. I understand that the items referred to by Mr. Currie in his report total in the neighbourhood of $50,000, much of which has been recovered. I am not talking about the horses that were referred to at Petawawa, but it does seem to me that at this time we are simply beating a dead horse.
The amount not recovered is no more than $15,000 or $20,000, and up to the present time we in this house have used $70,000 worth of time debating. We had better cut this out if we have any interest in the Canadian public dollar. If the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and members of the opposition parties are interested in saving money they should stop talking and get down to business and, at the earliest opportunity, see what this Currie report has to say.

Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I should like to speak for one moment on the subamendment proposed by the C.C.F., and make the position of the Social Credit group clear to the house. Members of our group have not done overmuch talking about the Currie

Committee on Defence Expenditure report. I think I am correct when I say that thus far only three of us have entered into the debate. I spoke very briefly when the report was tabled, I think on December 16, and placed our position before the house as clearly as I could, having had only a brief time in which to examine the recommendations of Mr. Currie. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas) spoke on January 15 and outlined our position a little more fully. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) spoke on January 16 and expanded somewhat on what had been said already.
Let me make it clear that the members of our group have not felt that we should strain at this matter. We felt that it was our responsibility to examine most carefully into the report and to see what could possibly be done to correct or help to correct the situation that has developed within the army works services. We felt right from the beginning that in his report Mr. Currie had revealed a shocking state of affairs within the army works services, a state of affairs that has caused considerable uneasiness to the people from one end of Canada to the other, a state of affairs that has resulted in the loss of many thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money.
We have tried to keep a balance in all that we have said or done in connection with the report and in the part we have taken in the debate thus far. We do not want to go overboard in an effort to make of this an election or political issue because we felt that we would like to know all that we could possibly learn about both sides of the question. We have felt that the government has been at fault in a good many ways and we have felt that to merely correct the accounting system and the security system which had been allowed to become loose and lax is not enough.
We have stated from the beginning that we felt that after doing everything possible to tighten up and improve the army works services accounting and administration systems, the government should then undertake a thorough and complete investigation of the whole Department of National Defence in all its branches from one end of the country to the other. We feel that it is necessary to investigate all branches of the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production to see if there are not other places where a saving of the taxpayers' money could be effected.
The hon. member for Red Deer has pointed out on two different occasions that he has evidence which indicates that there must be serious losses in connection with defence


construction, which evidence he is prepared to present at the proper time. We call upon the government to institute a wide investigation into defence construction activities from one end of the country to the other, into the granting of contracts and all that sort of thing that needs to be investigated. We are satisfied that much more serious losses will be revealed than have been revealed at Petawawa.
As a consequence we felt that we could not lay undue emphasis upon the Currie report, particularly in view of the fact that the government has given evidence that it is trying to close up the gaps, to tighten up the administrative and accounting systems which will make impossible the things that have happened in the past and which were revealed in Mr. Currie's report.
We did not enter into the discussion with respect to how a copy of the report got into the hands of the C.C.F. We felt that was a matter which did not concern us too greatly. All I can say is that I am most thankful that nobody came to me and offered me an advance copy of the report. I am glad that I did not have it. It was soon enough for me to get it when it was tabled in the house. Entirely aside from who was responsible and whether it was stolen or not, we felt that we should not help to bog down the discussion in this house on a matter that did not cen-cern us too much.
What does concern us is what can be done from here on. We do not think that a mere consideration of defence expenditures by a committee of this house is enough. We feel that nothing short of a complete judicial inquiry into all phases of defence expenditures and commitments, including defence construction, will suffice. I think the people of this country are demanding just that sort of thing. They are certainly getting tired of hearing of horses and nags and all the other things that have been bandied about for some weeks. They want action and I think they expect this house to settle down to business now and get action as quickly as we possibly can.
At first, Mr. Speaker, we felt that we could not support the C.C.F. subamendment because it did not go as far as we wanted it to go. We felt that merely asking Mr. Currie to continue an investigation in the field of defence expenditures and commitments was not nearly enough and we did, as I say, call for a full judicial inquiry into all phases of defence expenditures and commitments. However, since the first speeches were given in the house on the Currie report we have listened carefully and have tried to measure as carefully as we possibly could all of the evidence. A number of things have been

brought out that have changed our views a bit, and we find ourselves at the present moment in favour of the C.C.F. subamendment and will vote for it as the next best thing to a judicial inquiry.
It does not seem possible to get a judicial inquiry out of the discussion that we are carrying on here at the present time. Therefore we are prepared to support the C.C.F. subamendment, and we hope that the committee will get down to business as quickly as possible and will not only investigate the Currie report but will launch out and investigate all these other things that a good many of the members, including the hon. member for Red Deer, would like to have investigated. I name particularly defence construction contracts.

That the motion be amended by inserting after the words "March 31, 1950", in the fourth line thereof, the following:
"and initially to give priority in their examination to the expenditures and commitments of the Canadian army works services as dealt with in the report of G. S. Currie, Esquire, chartered accountant, tabled in the House of Commons on December 15, 1952."
There is nothing said here about referring the Currie report to the committee. What it does state is that the items referred to in the Currie report be examined by the committee, and, indeed, be given priority, which is a very different thing.
We are voting against the amendment because it does not refer the Currie report to the committee. It does not instruct the committee to consider the recommendations in the Currie report. All it does is instruct the committee, as its first task, to inquire into the very same matters as Mr. Currie has already inquired into. I maintain, Mr. Speaker-I am not allowed to impute motives -that the only result of the adoption of this amendment will be to prevent the committee doing anything except to hash over what has already been hashed over in this house for the last two weeks. That is the purpose of the amendment, and it could have no other purpose.
Why does the government want that to be done? As has been said, the government wants that to be done because, while the government accuses the opposition of playing politics with this report, the government is going to play politics with the report the moment that report comes into the committee. For that reason every member in this house who is interested in the honest administration of this country's affairs, every member in this house who feels appalled, as the general public feels appalled, at what was revealed in the Currie report should, regardless of his party affiliation, vote against this amendment. If there needs to be anything further done in that regard, it should have been done by adopting the amendment moved by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
Regrettably, it seems to me, the government has tried to belittle the Currie report; to make light of it and to laugh at it.


No matter how generous we want to be to the Department of National Defence, what was revealed in the Currie report is most appalling and should be considered seriously by this government. I should like to have spoken at length on this matter, and if the debate had continued a little longer I would have done so. If the government wants the people of this country to believe that they are interested in the honest administration of the Department of National Defence, for which the people of Canada are paying such a large amount of their taxes, not only for the defence of this country but for the defence of the free world, they should stop this quibbling, this manoeuvring for political position, and let this house and the government get at the facts.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my remarks only to the amendment before us and to the reasons why that amendment will be opposed by myself and, I believe, by the members of the party to which I belong. We have already indicated quite clearly that we disapprove strongly of this amendment and the manner in which it was introduced. It is accepted that this procedure is within the rules; nevertheless it establishes a highly unsatisfactory practice. In order to vote for a wider inquiry, it became necessary for us to support a subamendment which embraced the motion now before us. I explained why we would vote for the subamendment as we have voted for it. The amendment is now before us and I propose to vote against that amendment. In doing so, however, there are one or two points I wish to emphasize and I also wish to deal with a point raised this afternoon.
Some attempt was made to suggest a measure of inconsistency by reference to a motion made in the committee on defence expenditure on April 29 last by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness). The motion which has been referred to was a motion consisting of four paragraphs, one of which dealt with Mr. George S. Currie and the report he was to present. I submit that the way in which this reference has been introduced at this time is merely indicative of the extent to which the government and its supporters refuse to face the reality of the situation which is before us. Every device by which attention can be diverted from the real issue is employed by those who should be insisting upon a full inquiry if any of the arguments they made at that time in that committee had any real validity at all.
They opposed this motion for many reasons. They opposed this motion and voted it down

in the same way that every attempt before that committee to get facts was voted down. But anyone with any desire to understand the facts would know perfectly well that the motion as presented contemplated the return of the report by Mr. Currie during the life of that committee a year ago. The motion could have had no other meaning and no other thought. That was a year ago. The government did not want that report then; its supporters on the committee did not want that then. This man they had appointed was going to conduct an inquiry which would answer all these questions. They chose that course. They have received that report which is before us; and now a year later they suggest that it is wise for them to follow a course which they considered unwise a year ago.
Their inconsistency is this. If they really wanted to get at the facts, then was the time to do it. But no; they welcomed the postponement. They received the report. They delayed as long as possible its presentation to this house. Then when the report is before us they seek, by every device possible, further to postpone action on this report and also to prevent the possibility of that wider inquiry which is the only thing that we really need now.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has emphasized a point which might well be borne in mind by every hon. member of this house who will for a moment think of what we are really dealing with at this time. We are dealing with the preparation of the defences of Canada, the taxpayers' money, and the possibility of ending the extravagance, waste and theft disclosed by the Currie report. That is what we are dealing with. Every cent that is wasted; every cent that is lost by the theft of goods; every cent that disappears as a result of the wholesale looting which took place means added taxes to the people of Canada. That is one of the reasons why this matter calls for a wider inquiry into the whole field covered by the administration which invited theft and looting of this kind.
The hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out that this resolution now before us does not refer the Currie report to the committee but that it refers, for prior consideration of the committee, the subjects dealt with by Mr. Currie in conducting his inquiry which was the basis of this report. If the hon. members of this house support this resolution, they should recognize the fact that they are passing a resolution which is designed to sidetrack the Currie report and to conduct another inquiry into the same area, 68108-'794
Committee on Defence Expenditure although that inquiry was denied when the proposal was made by the hon. member for Calgary East before the defence expenditure committee on April 29 last year.
Let us once again recall what it is that is under consideration. A man with a distinguished record in the army in the first world war, with a high reputation as an accountant and with a respected reputation as deputy minister of national defence during the last war, undertook this task at the request of the government and conducted the inquiry they directed. They chose this great man, as they described him. We have accepted their estimate of that man. We are consistent in our acceptance of that estimate by saying that this man, with the qualifications which he possesses, should be permitted to extend that inquiry into the remaining part of the area of administration of the Department of National Defence which will expend this year over $2 billion of the taxpayers' money.
If that man was the great man described by the government, and if they accept even in a substantial measure the accuracy of his findings, then surely the first obligation of this government to our young men and young women in uniform and to the taxpayers whose money is being wasted and squandered, as disclosed in this report, is to appoint Mr. Currie to carry forward the investigation into every nook and cranny of a department whose administrative supervision of its responsibilities has broken down in the manner described.
That is what should be done. This motion is simply further delaying action by the government. It is drafted in a way that permits the government to sidetrack the report itself, to point to the wording of the report and say, "What you are told to consider in this committee is the subject matter that Mr. Currie dealt with, and to make your findings on that subject matter."
This house has debated the question for some time. Various opinions have been expressed. The answer of the government is, first of all, that the report of Mr. Currie in certain cases uses exaggerated language to describe events; and moreover, in so far as it makes recommendations, the government says in effect, "We have done most of these things that are suggested."
If this last assertion were so, then what earthly use would there be in having a further inquiry into a subject matter already covered by the report? Obviously if the government has acted, then that is finished business. The two arguments do not go hand in hand; it is one or the other.
The fact is that appropriate action has not been taken. The fact is that appropriate

Committee on Defence Expenditure action has not followed the findings. The fact is that there is no assurance and that there can be no assurance in the minds of the people of Canada that this long inquiry by this highly regarded expert is to produce any effective results on behalf of the heavily burdened taxpayer, or for the men and women in the uniform of Canada who are serving in different parts of the world today.
The government may not welcome repetition; it may not welcome discussion of this subject; but once again I urge every hon. member to recognize the evasive way in which this motion has been drawn and to vote according to his conscience. May I also urge that even at this late stage in the debate the government accept its responsibility, its duty to the men and women in uniform, its duty to the people of Canada, and say that it will direct Mr. Currie, or someone of equal competence, to continue this investigation into the large area not yet touched, and make a report which can result in savings of scores of millions of dollars to the taxpayers of Canada, as well as greater efficiency in the administration of that department upon which our security depends.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is an inquiry that might profitably be pursued. However, my purpose in rising at this time is not to deal with these very interesting aspects of the matter but with a matter of real substance on which, as I say, there seems to be a difference of opinion between the Department of National Defence and the Auditor General. Before I go into that, may I say a few words of a general character about this mimeographed document entitled "Background material". I have no quarrel with any person, department or organization coming to its own defence when attacked; but it does get a bit monotonous to discover that, so far as the Minister of National Defence and his department are concerned, they are always right. It does not matter what complaint is made, it does not matter what criticism is levelled, there is always a perfect answer, so far as the minister is concerned. Therefore when the Auditor General's report was tabled in the house on Monday, January 12, that same day the press was put in a position to carry answers from the Department of National Defence to every paragraph in the report of the Auditor General that referred to that department.
The answers all make it clear, of course, that what the Department of National Defence had done was really all right or it

Committee on Defence Expenditure was by understanding with the treasury board or that the matter had been sufficiently dealt with. However, let me get down to the issue in the dispute between the Auditor General and the Department of National Defence which I think is the most important one. It is found in paragraphs 56, 57 and 58 of the Auditor General's report which appear on pages 24 and 25 thereof. These paragraphs, the numbers of which I have just given, deal with several questions but in the main they deal with the manner in which the auditing of stores is conducted by the defence department. Mr. Watson Sellar, the Auditor General, points out in paragraph 56 (b) the following:
Long-term usage is to regard stores as service property with responsibility for accounting and custody vested in various components of the service forces. The consequence is that no civilian authority answerable to parliament exercises direct control after procurement.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the light of what has happened, which we have been discussing in relation to the Currie report, and in the light of the importance of parliamentary control over monetary and financial matters, I submit that this is a very important question upon which the Auditor General has put his finger; namely, that the set-up in the Department of National Defence is now such that these stores, the purchase of which parliament authorizes, which can run into millions and hundreds of millions of dollars, are being checked and audited by a system which is removed from direct responsibility to parliament.
In the document to which I referred, and which I originally called a blast back at the Auditor General, the Department of National Defence makes it clear that Mr. Watson Sellar is perfectly correct in his analysis of the situation. It is made clear from both these documents that what we have is a situation something like this. The deputy minister of national defence is regarded as responsible only to see and to satisfy himself that the chiefs of each of the services, the chiefs of staff, have an auditing system which is satisfactory. Beyond that, the responsibility for auditing and the responsibility for the care of these millions and hundreds of millions of dollars worth of goods that have been procured rests solely with the chiefs of the various staffs. In other words, if I may quote the language of the Winnipeg Free Press which happens to be on the side of the Auditor General and against the Department of National Defence in this matter, the deputy minister by this set-up has been reduced to the status of an errand boy.


The Department of National Defence, in my view, completely missed the point in Mr. Watson Sellar's paragraph 56 (b), because their answer to it in "Background material" is just a very simple sentence which reads:
The minister of the department is answerable to parliament for the stores held by the services.
It seems to me that is a very academic statement to make. The minister can stand up and say that he is responsible for everything that goes on in his department and all that sort of thing, but after the goods have disappeared, after it has turned out that the auditing system does not meet the scrutiny of an eye like that of Mr. Watson Sellar, or the scrutiny of Mr. Currie, it is not much use for the minister to say to parliament or through this memorandum that he is responsible.
The Winnipeg Free Press, as I say, deals very fully with this in an editorial which appeared in the issue of Saturday, January 17, 1953. It quotes in that editorial the main part of paragraph 56, together with some other material in that section of the Auditor General's report; and it also quotes the reply which was made by the Department of National Defence in its document entitled "Background material". After having quoted the pertinent paragraph from "Background material", the Winnipeg Free Press goes on to say:
With all deference to whoever wrote the foregoing. it must be said that to discard, demote or nullify the deputy minister in this fashion, the present law notwithstanding, is a reversal of sound practice. Moreover, to exalt the chiefs of staff in this way is to revert to the commander-in-chief principle of military organization which consistently and disastrously failed in Great Britain and was finally abandoned early in the present century. To abolish this chief of staff mastery was, perhaps, the greatest achievement of the famous Haldane reorganization and reform of the British army. It is shocking to discover that such antiquated ideas of army, air force and navy organization not only exist but are in operation at Ottawa.
The paragraph in the material from the Department of National Defence which the Free Press is criticizing, in the quotation which I have just read, is a paragraph which reads in part as follows:
The point which the Auditor General is endeavouring to make is obscure.
Well, right off the bat these anonymous spokesmen for the Department of National Defence admit that they did not understand the point that was being made by the Auditor General, so I do not see why they should so readily rush into print with an answer to it. They go on to say:
Stores purchased for the Canadian forces may only be used for those forces except where parliament has given authority for their use for other

purposes. Parliamentary grants do not distinguish between moneys for reserve stores and maintenance stores nor would it be desirable to segregate these for the reasons given with reference to audit note No. 56. In so far as a distinction between service and departmental accounting responsibilities is concerned, each chief of staff is responsible under the National Defence Act for the control and administration of his service.
That is the position taken by the Department of National Defence with respect to the care for these huge quantities of stores, that each chief of staff is responsible; not the deputy minister, not the minister, but the chiefs of staff.
Let me go on and indicate a point I made a moment ago, namely that the minister of the department takes the view that the only responsibility of the deputy is to be satisfied as to the kind of accounting system that the chiefs of staff are using. This is the position taken by the department:
If by departmental, the Auditor General has reference to the deputy minister and his staff, the responsibility of this officer extends only to an examination on behalf of the minister of the manner in which the accounting operations are being carried out by each service.
That is the statement, that is the view that is advanced of what is going on in the Department of National Defence which even the very Liberal Winnipeg Free Press *cannot take and against which it has made the comment in the paragraph I quoted from that paper a moment ago.
I recognize that the language I used when I referred to this material as a blast may have been offensive to the minister, but it was not uncalled for. I am still puzzled as to how that department was in a position, so soon after the tabling of the Auditor General's report, to make these replies of theirs to points in the report. I am even more puzzled, if Arthur Blakely's comment is correct, over the fact that some newspapermen had this background material from the department, these answers to the Auditor General's report, even before they had the Auditor General's report itself.

I am very glad to hear that explanation from the minister. He now tells us that the request for this information came to the department during the morning of January 12, and that the material was prepared and made available to them by six o'clock that evening. The Auditor General's report, of course, was tabled in this house at 2.30 o'clock that afternoon. Well, that is efficiency which we do not always find in the Department of National Defence, in that it was possible between 2.30 in the afternoon when that report was tabled and six o'clock to prepare and distribute an eight-page mimeographed document answering in technical language all the technical points set out in the Auditor General's report.
However, Mr. Speaker, I leave that part of the matter for those interested to pursue; but I do raise this matter of substance in the hope that the committee will go into it very carefully. It seems to me it may well be that one of the reasons we have had the scandals at Petawawa, one of the reasons we have had the things exposed that were revealed in the Currie report, is this kind of set-up with respect to these stores where there is that gap in responsibility between the civilian authority, namely the deputy minister acting for his minister on the one hand, and the chiefs of staff on the other. We urge very strongly that there should be no diminution of the practice of the principle of parliamentary control over the moneys we vote, and over the use of the stores that are purchased with that money. Parliamentary control of these stores must not disappear or be diminished in any way. That is what has happened as a result of this change in the set-up in the department. In my view the position should be changed back again at the earliest possible date, so there will be a complete responsibility for the auditing at the level where there is direct responsibility to parliament.
I recognize what this may mean in terms of more work at the deputy ministerial level. I realize what it may mean in terms of more work at the ministerial level. It may require more deputy ministers or it may require more ministers in the Department of National Defence, if this department is going to be such big business as it is. But in terms of parliamentary authority over these things there is a principle here that we simply must not let go. I recognize the tremendous amount of work and physical labour that must be involved when the minister has to sign his name hundreds of times every day. Even so, I think we were all amazed to have him tell us that he had not looked at any of the reports of the chief auditor in his own department, and that the deputy minister had looked at only a few of them.

Committee on Defence Expenditure
When you add all those things together, that lack of concern in studying these reports and the fact that this gulf has been created between the responsibility of the minister and the responsibility of the chiefs of staff, you have a situation which I suggest may have helped create the open doors referred to in Mr. Currie's report. One of the things that interest me about the Auditor General's report is the way he can deal with very important issues in the most moderate language. I find, for example, that his language in paragraph 58 is most restrained. He says:
Once procurement has been completed, it is the practice in some commonwealth countries-
Implying there that it has not yet been recognized as the practice in Canada.
-to regard issues for immediate requirements of the services as outside parliament's concern; all other holdings are regarded as still of parliamentary interest.
Then he shows the basis upon which that decision has been taken in some commonwealth countries, but not in Canada. He goes on to say:
Should this view-
The view that there are certain stores that are beyond parliamentary concern.
-be regarded as suited to Canadian requirements, attention is drawn to the need for the establishing of a dividing line between service and departmental accounting responsibilities.
In other words, Mr. Sellar admits that government policy is not his business. He merely comments on what is happening, and government policy rests with the government and whatever it can get through parliament. It seems to me that paragraph 58, taken along with paragraphs 56 and 57, indicates very clearly that, so far as Mr. Sellar is concerned, he does not approve of this practice of drawing a line between the two types of stores and allowing this huge quantity of stores to get into places where it is beyond accounting scrutiny that is directly responsible to parliament.
It is that issue which prompted the Winnipeg Free Press, in its editorial of January 17, 1953, on the defence department, to express the hope that the practice now being followed will be changed. The Winnipeg Free Press says:
Whatever else it may do, "Background Material" proves conclusively that there are grave weaknesses in the present organization of the Department of National Defence."
This is what I am talking about now. For the moment I am not complaining against any persons. I am not even repeating my complaint about the attitude of the top brass, and that sort of thing. What I am talking about now is the organization. Perhaps the minister
[.Mr. Knowles.]
will say this is provided for in the new National Defence Act. The Free Press admits that may be the case, and says if that is so then the act ought to be changed. The editorial goes on:
Would it be asking too much of the members of the government that they study the Esher report, the Haldane reforms, such textbooks on military as those written by the late Spenser Wilkinson, the former Chichele professor of military history at Oxford and examine the present organization of the British army, air force and navy?
There is a long, interesting, and exceedingly rewarding history in this regard and quite clearly the structure of our defence department at Ottawa is faulty.
Army organization is not and should never be a party or political matter. It is not a case of votes or constituencies. The need is for efficiency in the armed services and "Background Material"-
That is this document which was prepared and made public on the day the Auditor General's report was laid on the table of parliament.
-indicates all too clearly that our air force, army and navy are organized upon lines which make efficiency unattainable.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the charges in that editorial in one of the most prominent Liberal newspapers in the country, the Winnipeg Free Press, provide an even greater challenge to the government, and to the defence expenditure committee, than the Currie report or the Auditor General's report. There is a clear suggestion that the organization that is now in effect, particularly with respect to the handling of these huge quantities of stores, in the words of the Free Press, "makes efficiency unattainable". I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the defence expenditure committee will go into this important phase of the matter and make appropriate recommendations back to parliament.

We will support the motion to set up this committee. In doing so, however, and in spite of the amendment which has been passed which ties the hands of that committee to some extent, I would hope that on this occasion the committee will make a serious effort to open up an inquiry into the accounts and not continue to be the kind of whitewashing committee which it has been in the past.
In view of the statement that has been repeated by members of the government to the effect that the defence expenditure committee has dealt with certain questions on certain occasions and found everything to be

satisfactory, I should like to remind hon. members that no minority report is permitted from committees of this house. With respect to the defence expenditure committee, in many cases the majority reports have not represented the opinions of the members of other parties.
This is not the time to discuss the rules of the house. I would hope that before this committee deals with the subject matters which come before it and is ready to report, the government will give consideration to the advisability of making provision for minority reports. In this way there could be an expression of opinion on the part of those who seek to place before the house ideas as to the way in which changes could be made for the benefit of the people of Canada. This committee can perform a great service if it is free to do so. But past experience is not encouraging. I urge the government to take off the shackles and indicate its desire, so that the measure of the uniformity of opinion which has so often asserted itself on the part of members on the other side might conceivably assert itself again to the advantage of the people of Canada rather than to the advantage of this government.
