speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on November 24 last I laid on the table order in council P.C. 4553 which had been passed that day. This order designated the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) as a person who, under the terms of section 5 of the National Defence Act, might exercise any power or perform any duty or function that is vested in or that may be exercised or performed by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I think hon. gentlemen will find at page 15 of Hansard the statement I made on tabling that order in council. At that time I drew hon. members' attention to the forecast of legislation made in the speech from the throne, to provide for an associate minister of national defence. And as hon. members will recall I dealt with the desirability of having an associate minister of national defence, and foreshadowed the legislation to be introduced in consequence of this resolution. I have little to add to what I said on that occasion.
As I pointed out, a number of countries at the present time have, in addition to an overall minister of national defence, a minister for each of the three services, the navy, the army and the air force. That is the situation, I understand, in the United Kingdom, in the United States, in France and in Australia.

We have, however, considered it preferable in Canada to stress unification of the services for purposes of administration under the control of a single minister, a single department and a single deputy minister. We believe that our system has demonstrable advantages for this country, and that the appointment of separate ministers for each of the three services would be a retrograde step.
In the United States even today it is the view of the Hon. Robert A. Lovett, secretary of defence, who has just retired after quite a long experience in the defence department of that country, that the department has not had and still does not have sufficient power to bring about that degree of unification and co-ordination which was aimed at when their present national security act was adopted in 1947, or even when it was substantially amended in 1950.
In consequence of the course we adopted we have, I believe, gone as far to bring unification and co-ordination to the armed forces as have any of the free countries. While that is so, additional ways of developing unification and co-ordination still further are the subject of constant consideration.
As I said, it was hoped, and it was even expected, that the volume of work required of the minister would have become lighter as the defence program developed. That has not proved to be the case. Unfortunately the prolonging of the conflict in Korea, the buildup of our forces in Europe, and our relations with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, as well as greatly increasing the responsibilities of administering the department have also made it necessary quite frequently for the minister to be absent from the country. Our experience has shown that in a country like Canada the Minister of National Defence cannot administer the department and supervise the armed forces adequately by spending his whole time here in Ottawa.
Perhaps I should add a word or two to indicate just what there is to be administered and supervised. Reading on the globe, from left to right, as they do in photographs, we have the 25th Canadian infantry brigade in action in Korea, including various supporting units and details, back to the former capital of Seoul, where there are a number of units including a hospital, and then back to the base unit at Pusan, which is the main harbour.
To the west of Korea, in the Yellow sea, there are usually stationed three destroyers of the Royal Canadian Navy, making active contact with the enemy. They are based in Japan, over 100 miles to the east.
Not far back, at Kure, Japan, is the reinforcement group and other supporting details of the 25th brigade. At Kure also is the corn-68108-80i
National Defence Act
monwealth division's hospital, with a number of Canadian doctors and nurses, and, unfortunately, several Canadian wounded men. Not far from Kure there are training grounds where officers and men receive final training before going up to the front lines. Some 400 miles to the northeast of this is Tokyo, where there is a leave centre, a recreation room, and joint staff mission. Here also is the Japanese end of the Far Eastern airlift of the R.C.A.F., which has supporting details at Shemya in the Aleutian islands, as well as at McChord field in the state of Washington.
Then across Canada we have the various administrative training and operational units of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian army and the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Units of the navy train by being at sea, and of the air force by flying. Their training and operations have taken the R.C.N. and the R.C.A.F. into most quarters of the globe during the year.
However, resuming our glance from left to right, we come to the R.C.A.F. wing at North Luffenham and the depot at Langar in England. Also in England we have the joint staff mission and a very considerable number of members of all three services either on exchange duties or attending courses and taking training. In addition there are British and United States service personnel in Canada for similar purposes.
Then in Germany we have the 27th brigade located at three different camps around Hanover but often away in different parts of Germany on exercises. This year we hope it will take up permanent quarters of its own at Soest, halfway between Hanover and Cologne, and we shall establish base detail in Belgium.
In France there is a second wing of the R.C.A.F. at Grostenquin and the air division headquarters at Paris, soon to be established at Metz. We shall soon have a Canadian component in the 4th allied tactical air force of which our air division will form a part.
In Paris also we have our representatives, civil and military, to NATO, and a certain number of Canadian officers at SHAPE.
In a month or two we will have a third wing of the R.C.A.F. at Zweibrucken and later this year a fourth wing at Bad Solingen in Germany.
I mention this because today we have members of all three services engaged in the threefold task of supporting United Nations action in Korea, taking our part under the North Atlantic treaty and engaged in the defence of Canada, involving relations with

National Defence Act
more countries than ever has been the case for this country in war or in peace.
Canadian forces are in Korea, Japan, the United States, Britain, Germany, Belgium and France. This situation is new. We have to work out with all these, as we call them, "host countries" agreements regarding jurisdiction over civil and criminal matters, customs duties and other taxes, passport and immigration regulations, postal and transport arrangements, tenure of land and maintenance of buildings, and numerous other questions of the greatest complexity and importance. This has involved endless negotiation at every level, and I am glad to say that the arrangements we have made have generally proved quite satisfactory.
Largely because of the increasing importance of such matters, we found it necessary some time ago to appoint a chairman of the chiefs of staff committee. A large part of his time is devoted to dealing with matters of joint co-operation in NATO, and with other countries, at the highest service levels.
In addition to these matters which are to a considerable extent political, constitutional and legal, there are other matters regarding standardization, the exchange of information on development, research and doctrine, the development of channels of communication and co-operation which require attention not only at the service level but also at the political level.
In all this I may say Canada has taken a very considerable part, and there is every indication that this kind of work will increase rather than diminish.
Within Canada the basic program has been laid down, and I think and hope the majority of the contracts for construction and equipment has been placed. It now seems possible to see a clearer division between matters of policy and matters of administration or of the implementation of policy.
Therefore it seemed to the government that this situation would make it possible to have the responsibility shared between ministers, and that that could best be done by the appointment not of three ministers of defence over the separate services but of one associate minister of national defence. The minister and associate minister will work closely together in all matters. One will take the place of the other when the other has to be away attending conferences, visiting our forces abroad or in points in Canada away from headquarters. The experience of the present minister would indicate that this is apt to take about one-third of one man's time.

The main line of division will be that the minister will usually attend to matters having to do with defence relationships with the United Nations, with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, with countries of the commonwealth and with the United States. He will also usually take the initiative with respect to matters of policy within Canada relating to defence generally or to two or more of the three services.
The associate minister, in addition to carrying on the work of the minister when the minister is away, will keep more closely in touch with matters of administration relating to the services. If I may repeat, it is expected that the associate minister would act for and exercise the powers of the minister when the minister is away and deal with matters of administration relating to the three services, including requisitions for construction, equipment and supplies, submissions on similar matters to the governor in council and to the treasury board, control of the establishment, appointment and supervision of the civil employees and service personnel, approval of expenditures, orders, instructions and plans within the lines of agreed policy.
When they consider the magnitude of the task of presiding over the department hon. members will probably ask themselves why an associate minister was not designated before now. Certainly the question has been raised in a not altogether friendly fashion by at least one newspaper and perhaps also elsewhere. However, it will be recalled that immediately after the war, and indeed right up to the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, our defence program was less than a quarter of what it is now. In addition, we felt it desirable to emphasize as much as we could the unification of the services for administrative purposes. Even with the coming of war in Korea and the rapid planned build-up of forces for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, it was not for some time that the pattern of our defence effort came to be worked out. There was much discussion and revision of plans and programs.
While the load of work borne by the Minister of National Defence was very great it was not clear, until the greatly enlarged program got under way, how best to divide the responsibilities of the defence department. We were not getting into a full-scale war but we were certainly into something which was not normal peace; and while plans for the build-up were being made it would not, I think, have been wise to divide the constitutional ministerial responsibility for meeting the many grave problems which arose from day to day in building up our defence forces.

Having now settled the main lines of our defence effort and having reached the principal decisions on policy, it has been possible to work out a plan for sharing the heavy load of responsibility in the manner envisaged in this legislation to provide for the appointment of an associate minister of national defence. I hope the plan will commend itself to the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister not going to explain to us why the act needs to be amended? That is what the motion proposes to the house, yet he has given no word of explanation as to why the act needs to be amended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The act needs to be amended because as it stands it provides that the governor in council may in an emergency appoint as many as three additional ministers of national defence; but only in an emergency. We do not think we are in the kind of emergency that would allow the governor in council to act under that statute and make appointments without further authority from parliament. We are now asking that, although there is not that kind of emergency, the governor in council may appoint an associate minister of national defence; and that while there is in office an associate minister of national defence the act which provides for the appointment of three additional ministers in an emergency be amended to provide for the appointment of two only.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I should like to ask one question before I make any further remarks. I understand the Prime Minister's reason for considering it expedient that we have this amendment is that the number should be reduced from three to one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The National Defence Act as it stands provides that in an emergency there can be an over-all minister of national defence and one separate minister for each of the three services. Here we wish to provide for the appointment of an associate minister of national defence who will not be identified with any one of the three services in particular but who will have powers that will extend to all three. We propose to ask the house to amend the provision in the statute by taking power to appoint an associate minister, even though there not be an emergency contemplated by the act. Secondly, we are asking to amend the provision which permits the appointment of three separate ministers by providing for the appointment of two only while there is an associate minister acting with the minister.

National Defence Act
emergency contemplated in the act, am I right in assuming that there is no difference between the emergency contemplated in this act and any other emergency?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: My understanding is that the emergency contemplated in the act is the kind of emergency defined in the War Measures Act; that is, the existence of war, actual or apprehended. We had quite a lengthy debate in this house when we introduced the first modified Emergency Powers Act immediately after the outbreak of war in Korea to take certain powers less than those that would result from the proclamation of the War Measures Act. We felt that there was not the kind of emergency existing at the present time that would authorize us to proclaim the War Measures Act or to exercise powers that are similarly to be exercised in the case of a situation described in the statute as an emergency.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has outlined the heavy duties that devolve upon the Department of National Defence, and has indicated the reasons which in his opinion support the contention that there should be an associate minister. But I submit that the amendment that is suggested is hardly supported by the arguments he has put forward. The reference to events in different parts of the world with which the Department of National Defence is connected does not in itself suggest a change in the situation which would support the need for an amendment of this nature at this time, unless there are some reasons which have not been placed before us.
I could understand an argument in favour of the appointment of a minister to deal with a specific service or to deal with specific duties in relation to the functions of the Department of National Defence. If the associate minister is, however, simply to have parallel duties to those of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), it seems that the purpose of the appointment-not the amendment but the appointment-is merely to give ministerial rank to a parliamentary assistant. The duties that have been described would be performed by a parliamentary assistant except in so far as attendance at cabinet meetings is concerned.
I doubt if any hon. member will question the fact that steps need to be taken to improve the situation. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said that many countries have ministers for each service. He has pointed out that this is the system adopted in the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Australia and other countries.

National Defence Act
He did go on to say that the government believes our system has advantages in bringing about co-ordination. I should think we have had abundant evidence in the past few days that it has produced the very opposite. I should think we have had abundant evidence in the past few days that what we greatly need is some new definition of the duties of those who will be responsible for administration. If there is to be an additional minister, then I submit that one of the things which should be before the house is a clear definition of the responsibilities of that minister. If his real duty is to be that of an administrative official with cabinet rank, then I believe that should be before us in some detail when we say that it is expedient to introduce an appropriate amendment for this purpose. If on the other hand it is to deal with a particular service, then I think that should be before us.
I should think that great advantages could accrue from the appointment of a minister to a particular service, even if at the present time it is only to take over one service. Having regard to the fact that special emphasis is being placed upon Canada's development of its air defences, I can well see reasons why we should have a minister of national defence for air, or, if the minister is to be appointed under section 6 of the army act, an associate minister specifically appointed to deal with the administration of that branch of our military services.
I must confess that I find it difficult to understand how the government can contend on this occasion that there is no emergency and that the act must be amended for that reason, if it proposes to come before us at a later time in the session and suggest that there is an emergency which calls for the introduction of two other bills referred to in the speech from the throne. Either there is an emergency or there is not. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said that this provision was made at a time when we contemplated a special type of emergency. Then he went on to say-and while I do not purport to quote his exact words I am sure I am quoting their effect-that while we were not in a full-scale war we were certainly in something other than normal peace.
The only amendment, Mr. Speaker, that is contemplated by the motion before us, the only amendment it is suggested we should declare ourselves to believe it is expedient to introduce, is that the restriction that this can be done by order in council in time of emergency shall be removed and that there shall be a provision that at any time an additional minister can be appointed by order in council. I submit that if there is no

emergency we should follow the normal method, and that a bill should be introduced to deal with the appointment of a new minister in the ordinary way. Otherwise it is open to the government to appoint a new minister by order in council at any time without the matter being submitted to parliament. If there is no emergency, then the ordinary procedure of creating a new ministry and describing its functions by statute should be employed.
If there is an emergency, then no amendment is required. Section 6 of the act as it stands is more than adequate for the purpose of dealing with the situation outlined by the Prime Minister. I should think that everything that has taken place in the house ever since we met this session would emphasize the need for the most exact procedure in dealing with all matters connected with the Department of National Defence. I do not think we should further increase the opportunity for informal proceedings and undefined authority.
For that reason I hope hon. members will realize that what we are asked to declare by this motion is that, in the opinion of the members of the house, it is expedient that at any time, without the house knowing anything about it, an additional minister may be appointed without the house having any opportunity to say whether or not it is wise and also without the house having any opportunity to say what the duties of that minister shall be. I hope that hon. members, with that before them, will oppose this motion.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) moved a resolution that it was expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Defence Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order. May I correct the hon. member? The motion that was moved was that the Speaker do now leave the chair. That is the motion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That in committee we should discuss this resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Defence Act to provide that the Governor General may at any time appoint an associate minister of national defence at a salary of ten thousand dollars per annum.
We feel this resolution unnecessary because we feel that the present act makes provision for the government to appoint such associate

minister if the government so desires. We also feel that in the remarks made by the Prime Minister the duties of this associate minister were ill-defined, vague and not sufficiently specific.
I think it would be advisable to quote the actual words of the National Defence Act, paragraph 6 (1):
The Governor General may, during an emergency, by a commission under the Great Seal appoint (a) not more than three additional ministers of national defence, each of whom shall exercise and perform such of the powers, duties and functions of the minister as may be prescribed by the governor In council;
That refers to the possibility of the appointment of additional ministers of national defence. When the Prime Minister was speaking, according to the notes I jotted down at the time, he said that the National Defence Act as it stands provides that in an emergency there can be an over-all minister of national defence and one separate minister for each of the three services. My interpretation of the act, as I have read it, is that it does not state definitely that these three ministers are to be allocated to each of the three services; because it says very distinctly:
-each of whom shall exercise and perform such of the powers, duties and functions of the minister as may be prescribed by the governor in council;
My interpretation of the duties of those three ministers, if appointed, is not so circumscribed as the interpretation given by the Prime Minister this afternoon.
Paragraph 6 (1) (b) of the act reads:
-not more than three associate ministers of national defence, each of whom shall exercise and perform such of the powers, duties and functions of the minister as may be assigned to him by the governor in council or the minister.
That is, if necessary in an emergency there may be appointed three associate ministers of national defence. Paragraph 6 (2) goes on to say that such minister-
-may be continued in office for not more than six months after the termination of the emergency during which he is appointed.
I must submit that a great deal of the Prime Minister's speech this afternoon indicated that an emergency does exist. He referred to the 25th brigade being in. action in Korea, and outlined the various establishments which are maintained in the Far East, not only for the army but also for the navy and the air force. He went on to describe how our 27th brigade is stationed in Germany and how various units of the Royal Canadian Air Force are also stationed in Europe. He pointed out that we had units of our defence forces in Korea, Japan, the United States, Britain, Germany, Belgium and
National Defence Act
France. Those units of our defence forces, be they of the army or air force, are stationed in Europe because the dread of war hangs over Europe.
We find that we have Canadian troops in the Far East because there is real war. The illusion that there is only police action in Korea surely has been shattered when we realize that there have been over 1,200 Canadian casualties in Korea, of whom some 245 have been killed. Surely nobody is trying to maintain the myth that there is not war in Korea. Of course there is war, and real war, in Korea.
So far as Europe is concerned the raison d'etre for our troops being in Europe is the threat of war; war is apprehended. In the definition of this act we are told that an emergency means war, invasion, riot or insurrection, real or apprehended. I do submit, then, that we are faced with real war in Korea and apprehended war in Europe. For these reasons I feel that there is an emergency, and therefore the paragraph of this act granting authority to appoint both additional ministers and associate ministers amply applies, and has applied for many months past. On that ground I feel that it is quite unnecessary to refer this resolution to any committee or to even present the resolution at all. I do not see how we can say on one hand there is war, and on the other hand that our troops in action in Korea are not taking part in active service operations there.
Then the Prime Minister referred to the fact that in a number of countries there were over-all ministers of defence. I believe he pointed to the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia and France as countries having over-all ministers of defence. He said also these ministers had under them subordinate ministers who were charged with the responsibility of supervision, administration and organization of definite services, or some specific job they had to do. For several years after the end of the last war, while the army and navy were combined under a minister of national defence, we still retained a minister of national defence for air. II is not, therefore, an unusual thing so far as this country is concerned, and so far as the policy of the present government is concerned, that there should be a separate minister for one or other of these services, with a definite job.
The Prime Minister said that it would be a retrograde step if we established separate ministers for each of the three services. 1 wonder whether the experience which has been gained by following this fetish of unification has really shown that the policy oi

National Defence Act
unification at the top has been entirely successful. I believe we have had ample demonstration recently that it is impossible to have unification throughout the administration of the services. There may be unification or an attempt at unification at the top, but we have not made any great progress in unification in the middle. Only a few days ago we heard that there were eight different accounting systems. In fact, if I recall correctly, it was suggested that there was no great harm in having various accounting systems in the service, and that we should not strive after unification for unification's sake.
I am not at all sure we have not stressed too greatly this necessity for unification starting at the top. True, we are trying the experiment at the bottom as well. We have the three combined service colleges in which cadets of the army, navy and air force are studying together. I do not think we have gone far enough yet to say whether that experiment is entirely successful. We must have liaison and co-ordination, most assuredly. There has to be co-ordination between all three services; there is no question about that.
Surely the Minister of National Defence, who we have been told must spend a large part of his time away from Ottawa conferring with other countries-conferring with the NATO commanders; conferring with the United Nations and so forth-with his broad experience of what is going on in other countries would be in an admirable position to co-ordinate the activities of our three services. Because he is away from Canada so much, and because his duties take him into the realm of diplomacy, into the management of international relations, experience has shown that he has not had sufficient time to devote to the administration of all services, the army, the navy, the air force and the defence research council. We have found that there have been reports of failure in the administration. In fact, a great deal of the present minister's time has been taken up with the management of international relationships as well as the management of interservice relationships. I submit that he is in a position to be able to continue with the general supervision over all three of our services.
In order to help him along these lines he has, within the last couple of years, appointed a chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, to whom the Prime Minister referred. Under that chairman there are the chiefs of staff of the navy, army, air force and research council. There you have co-ordination at the top; liaison by the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee with the chiefs of staff of every service. As I see it the present minister is in a position to exercise that general supervision, being the over-all minister, in

much the same way as the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee exercises general supervision over the chiefs of staff of the various services.
We do realize that it would be an enormous task for the present minister or any other minister to maintain the general supervision of all the services and carry on these international discussions and relationships. It is beyond human power to be able to do that. He does need, and has needed for a long time perhaps, additional assistants. He has been provided with parliamentary assistants for some time. Just how he has divided the responsibilities which are his amongst his parliamentary assistants is a matter for him to decide.
This afternoon we were told by the Prime Minister-and I use his words as closely as I could copy them down while he was speaking-that the associate minister would keep more closely in touch with matters of administration relating to the services, that he would keep in touch with the administration of the three services as well as acting for the minister when he was away. Of course, when one minister is away another minister always has to act in his place. Then the Prime Minister went on in a little bit more detail and said that, amongst his other administrative duties, he would be required to supervise requisitions for construction. As we know, there is a great deal of building going on for the three services. Construction is playing a big part and is taking a large portion of the money which is voted for defence purposes. The associate minister would also be responsible for supervision of civil employees in the department-of whom there are a great many-and also for appointments and for the approval of expenditures. There may have been some other details to which the Prime Minister referred but those are, in the main, the duties which he assigned to the associate minister.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is utterly impossible to separate administration from policy. If administration falls down, then the policy cannot be put into effect. Administration and policy go hand in hand; and it is exceedingly difficult to make one man responsible for administration and somebody else responsible for directing policy. I think everyone who has had any practical experience, either in the services or in business, will realize that policy and administration go together. I therefore foresee that there will be great difficulties confronting the associate minister of national defence if he is to devote his attention almost entirely to matters of administration.

It is essential that the load be taken of! the present Minister of National Defence. I know that is the truth. In fact, in this house I suggested, I think about a year ago, that the present minister could not undertake all the responsibilities in connection with civil defence; and I am pleased that, shortly after that suggestion was made by me, the government acted on it and transferred the duties of civil defence to another minister.
One man can do just so much. It is an unfortunate practice that we sometimes have of overloading the willing horse. Hence I suggest that in the past we have been asking too much of our Minister of National Defence and that some relief was due him long ago. If that relief is long overdue, let us be practical, and let us see what is the best way in which we can relieve him of some of this burden which has overtaxed human ability.
We must realize that the present Minister of National Defence has shown exceedingly great ability. I do not hesitate to pay my tribute to him for all that he has attempted to do. He has had to try to take in the broad picture. By inclination he is extremely keen on administrative detail; hon. members can see that inclination evidenced in the reports he has made to this house. He has almost a mania for detail. He will come here and give us a large number of figures representing the amounts of money which have been spent by this and that department. He will have them at the tips of his fingers. I think he has shown on many occasions a remarkable ability in being able to point out the details connected with the various services. I am afraid that, by inclination, he is going to follow on with that mania. He loves detail, and it is going to be tremendously hard for him to divorce himself from administrative detail.
We are obliged to rely upon him to give us the over-all picture, and to deal with the immense problems of international relationships, interservice policy and so forth. But if he ties himself down to details as well, we are not going to have this country adequately served in that respect. If only loose instructions are given to his associate minister to look after administration I am fearful that, during the two-thirds of his time that the Minister of National Defence will be looking after affairs in Ottawa he will, by sheer force of habit, delve into matters of administration. Hence I foresee an associate minister of national defence charged with the responsibility of administration and a minister of national defence finding it extremely hard to divorce himself from the details of administration because, as I have already pointed out, administration and
National Defence Act
policy are closely interrelated. I therefore fear that we shall have confusion worse confounded and that we shall just go on muddling along; because if the division of responsibility, as defined by the Prime Minister today, is adhered to we shall have no clear-cut solution to the problem.
I should like to see this resolution reconsidered and provision made for a definite area of responsibility to be allocated to this associate minister of national defence. If any additional help is required for the minister, then let further parliamentary assistants be appointed. As was suggested this afternoon by the leader of this party, I would suggest that at this time we might well appoint a minister of defence for air.
Let us just look for a few minutes at the responsibilities a minister of defence for air would have.
To begin with, let us consider the amount of money that this house allocated in the main estimates during the last year for the defence services. For air alone there was allocated the huge sum of $929 million plus $577,891, a total of $929,577,891. The administration of that huge sum of money certainly requires that there should be a separate minister to look after that particular service. If it were just in the ordinary course of events that this large sum of money was being provided for our air service, perhaps the need would not be emphasized to the same extent as it is when one looks back and takes note of the amount allocated in the main estimates of 1951, at which time the sum of $252,842,836 was set aside for this purpose.
So we see here an enormous increase in expenditure for the air force, an increase in one year from $252 million to $929 million. These figures must give hon. members some idea of the tremendous expansion and increase in our air defence. Surely we will not say that we are going to have just a flash in the pan, or that we are not going to stress the air service in the future.
On various occasions in the house I have stressed the necessity of placing emphasis upon our air defence. We are particularly suited to play a large part in air operations. We have an enormous country which can be defended only by rapid movement from one part of the country to another. Our air services are essentially for the defence of the country. Not only are they for the defence of Canada, but also to fulfil our obligations in other parts of the world, notably those under the United Nations. We have an air division either in or about to arrive in Europe. I think some 12 fighter

National Defence Act squadrons is the number that has been mentioned, and those squadrons are expected to arrive in Europe within the foreseeable future.
Then we have the NATO training scheme, in which we are inviting young airmen from other countries who have joined us in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to come to Canada so they may do their training here. We do this because we have the facilities for it.
We have our obligations in Korea where No. 426 transport squadron has been doing amazing work. As was disclosed recently, they have made over 350 crossings of the Pacific, both ways. They have flown over four million miles in transporting over 8,500 personnel.
Then, because of the stress being placed upon air forces the world over, the whole situation regarding air warfare is in a constant state of flux. Our responsible officials, be they service personnel or ministers of the crown, have tremendous obligations in order to keep up to date in matters of research, design and construction in connection with aerial warfare.
During the last war there was no question that Canada played a most effective part in aerial warfare. I think very few members in the house would question the statement that to a great extent our success was due to the energy and ability of the minister of defence for air of that time.
I feel the time has now come when we have to have a clear-cut understanding of the responsibilities and duties of this new associate minister, and that the logical, practical and realistic step to take is to say now, "We will revert to our wartime policy of having a separate minister for the air service," so that the activities of the air force with all its tremendous developments, and the administrative arrangements regarding personnel, as well as the provisions for modern types of aircraft with which it must be supplied, will be the responsibility of one individual.
In order to tie in those responsibilities and that development with the development and progress of our other defence forces, there would be the over-all minister of national defence, who would be able to spend his time dealing with his international responsibilities. Being relieved of air force responsibilities, and of the expenditure of these $929 million-almost half of the defence vote -with the assistance of such parliamentary assistants as he might deem necessary he would be able to look after the administration of the other two services, the army and the navy.


It is for these reasons we feel this resolution need not be submitted to a committee at this time. While we are opposed to the resolution for the reasons I have advanced, we feel it would be better to wait until the bill is before us to advance any amendments we may have in mind. I indicate to the Prime Minister the line of objection we shall take to the bill when it is presented, and I do this in the hope that he will give serious consideration to the arguments I have advanced, that he will realize the resolution is not necessary, that all the powers exist in the National Defence Act as it stands today, and that there is an emergency-and one cannot gainsay that there is a war in Korea and a war apprehended in Europe. If there is a real war in Korea and an apprehended war in Europe, an emergency exists. And if that emergency exists, then in the act he has all the power required to appoint whatever associate ministers he may need.
Finally I hope that a much clearer definition of the responsibilities of the associate minister will be placed before us. I do recommend with all sincerity that the simplest and most logical way of proceeding is to appoint either a minister or associate minister of national defence for air, and to divorce from the present minister all those details of administration, design, construction and development connected with the air services. I feel it will only add to the confusion if an associate minister is given responsibility in connection with administration, when his responsibility for general policy is limited.
I do not believe it will be possible for the Minister of National Defence to divorce himself entirely from matters of administration. I repeat that I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will see that it is not necessary to proceed with this resolution. Secondly, I hope that when the associate minister is appointed his duties will be clearly defined and that he will be made responsible for one service. I submit that the air service is the logical one to be given a minister rather than confuse the whole question by giving him some vague, ill-defined responsibility over the administration of the navy, army and air services, the northwest system and all the other administration details of national defence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am prompted to enter the debate at this time after having listened carefully to the recital which the Prime Minister gave us before the recess of the duties devolving upon the Minister of National Defence. I think he opened our eyes; but perhaps he should also have told us that the Minister of National

Defence handles nearly 50 per cent of the national expenditure. That is the responsibility of one man, whereas the other nineteen members of the cabinet look after the other 50 per cent of our national expenditure. It is the thought of the tremendous responsibility that is placed upon the Minister of National Defence that prompts me to say a few words tonight.
This department has always received the lion's share of our national revenue. As the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) just mentioned, the handling of this department has always been too much for one minister. I remember when this department was handled by my predecessor from Yale, the late Hon. Grote Stirling, in 1934 and 1935; and tonight I pay tribute to that hon. gentleman. He served for twenty years as a member of this house, and he acted also as minister of national defence. He gave of his best with untiring zeal during those twenty years. He was a fine gentleman, a good member of the house and a conscientious administrator. I still find in my correspondence reference to the work he did and the good deeds he performed. He passed away during last week end and I am glad of this opportunity to pay this tribute. He was honoured by all parties in the house.
It is with those thoughts in the back of my mind that I think of the heavy responsibilities that devolve upon the shoulders of one man. The division of duties will naturally be a contentious subject. We from British Columbia are pleased that one of our members has been selected as the associate minister, but at the same time we are not quite happy about the situation. The difficulty seems to me to be in the division of responsibility. From what we have heard, this -responsibility will still rest upon the one man. He will have an associate to help him, but previously he had a parliamentary assistant. He is not a great deal better off.
I think we as members of parliament should place direct responsibility on all our ministers. I do not care whether the department is divided into four ministries, but I do feel that the army, navy and air force require separate ministers. I should like to see consideration given to the appointment of a minister to handle administration matters, to clean up the mess exposed by the Currie report. I think it would be money well spent to have a minister to do nothing else but look into the bookkeeping system, the storage system, the security system, and to be personally responsible for those matters. Then other developments in the army, navy
National Defence Act
and air force could be under separate associate ministers if you wished. I realize that this may mean greater expenditures; but when you consider that half our national income is spent by this one department under one man, and the other half by the other nineteen members of the cabinet, I think the expenditure will be found to be justified.
That is all I have to say. I am not going to criticize the appointment because we from British Columbia are pleased with it. I think we have as good a man as we could find to fill the position. But I sincerely believe that definite responsibility should be placed on this individual rather than to make him just a glorified parliamentary assistant with increased pay.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that an associate minister will be of great assistance to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), although I contend there should be a more definite division of duties than was laid down this afternoon by the Prime Minister. I should like to see the new minister named as minister of air or as minister of air and navy, whichever is practicable, so there would be a more even distribution of responsibility.
This afternoon the Prime Minister said he did not like that kind of division because they were trying to retain as much unity as possible among the various branches of the service. But I would think if a break in that unity brought about increased efficiency it would probably be a good thing. If such a move would mean greater efficiency, then by all means we should have that definite break and have the duties of each of these ministers clearly defined.
We do not like to see a glorified parliamentary assistant in this post. We want to see a minister with definite duties. We want to see someone who can assume responsibility for certain branches of the department. I shall have to agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) in disagreeing with the method proposed by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister says that he does not believe there is an emergency, and therefore he does not have the power under the act to appoint other ministers.
I do not know whether I would agree with the Prime Minister that there is not an emergency. Our boys in Korea feel that there is some sort of emergency or they would not be fighting there. If the government is not willing to accept the fact that we are in a state of emergency, surely they will agree that at least the Department of National Defence is in a state of emergency. The

National Defence Act
events and debates of the last few days I think prove that pretty clearly.
If we are in a state of emergency then the government has the power to create one minister or three ministers, whichever number is needed. If there is no emergency then I am afraid I cannot agree that this is the type of action that should be taken. The position of the new minister should be created by statute and not in the manner that has been set forth in the house today.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a very few words, really to follow up what has been said by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes); but first I should like to make one or two general comments on the Prime Minister's speech. As I listened to the Prime Minister describing to us in his quiet persuasive tones the reason for the appointment of this new minister; as he described the scope of the duties of the present minister; as he took us from the front line in Korea to Pusan, to the destroyers in the sea of Japan, to the Aleutian islands, to Canada, to Britain, to Germany, to France and described in great detail-and I am sure accurately- the scope of the duties of the present minister, I said to myself: Is this really the month of January, 1953? What has been happening in the last two and a half years since July, 1950, when in effect the enormous nature of the commitments which we had undertaken became clear?
If the Prime Minister was trying to demonstrate to us that it was utterly impossible for one man to undertake these duties, I think he succeeded admirably; and the only thing I would say to the Prime Minister is that for many many months we on this side in our small way have been trying to persuade the government that that was so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: You are always right on your side.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
No, we are
not always right but we are sometimes right. We do not even suggest the government is always wrong, although they are sometimes wrong. What I want to come back to is that the government has taken advantage of the insatiable appetite for work and the insatiable energy of the Minister of National Defence; and in my opinion the government, and the Prime Minister at the head of it, are grievously to blame for the disorganization about which we now know, a disorganization which is demonstrated by the Currie report and which, if Mr. Currie could only investigate the whole of the expenditures instead of one one-hundredth, would be demonstrated even more.
We come now to this situation. I repeat that I think the government and the Prime Minister at the head of it are grievously to blame. Now the thing is to be set right; and how is it to be set right? Well, it seems to me that we are perhaps going from the frying pan into the fire. It seems to me we may be falling between two stools instead of falling off one stool. It seems to me that the outline of the duties that has been given does nothing whatever to indicate that there will be a clear-cut division. We were told by the Prime Minister this afternoon that the Minister of National Defence will usually look after duties A, B and C, let us say, and the associate minister will usually look after duties D, E and F, and that when one minister is away the other will look after his duties.
That is all right so far as it goes, but I submit it still leaves us in exactly the position outlined by the hon. member for Nanaimo, namely that there is no clear-cut definition of duties. We will still be in the position where energy and courage are asked to do the duty of organization. We have now found defects in the organization. We hoped that when the Prime Minister brought forward the resolution there would be evidence that there was now going to be some clear thinking to set this thing right. So far as I can see that evidence is not there. So far as I can see we are going to go on with the same vagueness, the same want of organization.
I hope, as the hon. member for Nanaimo has said, that the government will see fit to take another look at this matter. I hope in particular that they will accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Nanaimo, with all his experience and knowledge of these matters, as to a minister for air. In general it seems to me that he has made suggestions which, if we are single-minded in trying to correct this situation, the government might very well consider.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it quite clear that as far as this group is concerned we believe that the principle behind the resolution is good. We believe the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is in need of some assistance at this time. As a matter of fact, we think such assistance should have been given much earlier. We agree that when we sent our troops to Korea in the first place we did not expect that the war would drag on for two years, and that we probably thought then there might not be an emergency. But surely when we decided to become partners in NATO and to send a brigade to Europe, when we added to the responsibilities of the minister that of meeting the chiefs of staffs of

other countries and of consulting with the joint defence board set up in conjunction with the United States, it must have been apparent to the government that some assistance was necessary.
It should have been apparent to the government when our spending in this department practically tripled in one year that some assistance was necessary for the Minister of National Defence. Everybody agrees that the minister has done all that it was humanly possible for one man to do, but even that was not enough in the light of the tremendous responsibilities that devolved upon him so far as the increased expenditures and increased tensions in the world today are concerned. As I say, we agree with the principle that the minister should have assistance, but we do think it should be done in a somewhat different way than is being suggested.
In introducing the resolution the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated in a general way the division of responsibilities between the associate minister and the minister. He said the associate minister would be responsible for administration while the minister would be responsible for policy decisions and for attending international conferences and other meetings which our ministers of national defence must attend. That is not enough. When a government in this country appoints a minister of the crown and pays him the necessary emolument for that position, it seems to me that the minister as a member of the cabinet should be responsible to parliament for certain well-defined duties. After all, we still have a parliament, and it is parliament that is responsible to the people of the country, not the government alone.
How is parliament to hold the new minister responsible unless he has clearly defined duties? Therefore we say that in making this appointment the Prime Minister should clearly define the responsibilities that the associate minister is going to have. Surely there is some way in which the responsibilities involved in the Department of National Defence can be divided. Surely the matter of procurement and stores is a responsibility which might be given to the new minister at this time, because we are procuring tremendous quantities of goods and supplies not only for our armed forces as they are today but as they may be in the future. Surely there should be somebody directly responsible for that.
I am not going to try to define what division of responsibilities the government should make, but I say it should be clearly defined to parliament so that parliament can hold the minister appointed, whoever he may be, responsible for certain specific duties that he
National Defence Act
will have to perform as a member of the government. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) has suggested that the new minister might be made minister for air. That is a reasonable suggestion. In our defence department air responsibilities have always been great, in the last war and since the last war. We have taken on additional responsibility for the training of personnel from other parts of the NATO partnership, and those responsibilities are great.
I am not trying to say what the duties of the associate minister should be, but I do say they should be clearly defined by parliament so that when that minister is appointed parliament can hold him responsible for well-defined duties, as other ministers of the crown can be held responsible for their departments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I merely want to support the hon. and gallant member for Nanaimo with regard to a minister for air. If there is any way in which we -and I say "we" in the way the board of trade or chamber of commerce said "we as the third trading nation of the world"-have any responsibility in particular, it is our responsibility in the air. We have only a small population, and mass armies and large manpower are not for us. They can never be for us with our small population.
In two wars the Canadian genius showed us to be supreme in the air. I think the percentage of Canadians in the Royal Air Force and the Royal Flying Corps in the first war, and the Royal Air Force and the Royal Canadian Air Force in the second world war, was out of all proportion to our population. It is for that reason, for the logistics in the matter -one might almost say the geopolitical side -and also because of our peculiar genius for work in the air, that we should give special attention to it.
As has been said, expenditures for air defence have increased from a quarter of a billion to nearly one billion dollars. Not only have the expenditures increased; the technological progress in the air has increased at a very rapid rate and it is continuing to increase at even an accelerated rate at the present time.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that a minister for air, with the specific job of co-ordinating and co-operating with the air arm of the defence services, is an absolute necessity. Let us take what has happened recently. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was away attending a NATO conference. While he was away the Currie report was brought down and there was a great deal of confusion in the department. To have had

National Defence Act
a minister for air, or another defence minister, would have tremendously reduced that confusion and steps might have been taken immediately, rather than to have the very unfortunate time lag and time waste which took place.
So I say that a minister for air, not only because of our small population but because of our geopolitical position and because of the genius of Canadian people for work in the air, is an absolute necessity.
I feel that unification of the armed services is ideal, but it has never been effectively worked out in the United States or in the United Kingdom. Despite all high level conferences and all attempts to work out unification of defence forces, they still form themselves into three essential services. I understand it is the United Kingdom practice, and I think it is desirable, that a member for each service is appointed whose job is purely of a technical nature. He has the responsibility of reporting on technical matters directly to the cabinet, thereby taking off the shoulders of the ministers, who have other responsibilities in the house, the details of the technical problems of the services. I have been informed that that system has worked very well and has relieved ministers of a great many of these technical problems for which they have not been trained. So, Mr. Speaker, while the problem is to take as much of the technical responsibility and essential detail off the shoulders of the minister, I also feel that if we are increasing the cabinet it is essential that we increase it by a specific minister with specific duties. I suggest, in our peculiar position, a minister for air is one of the essential additions we should make to the cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, had it not
been possible for me to have this opportunity at once, I would have asked for the unanimous consent of the house to express to the hon. and gallant member for Nanaimo my sincere appreciation for the well-merited tribute he paid so generously, in a nonpartisan fashion, to the ability, energy and devotion to duty of the Minister of National

Defence. As a citizen of Quebec, I would also like to thank him for the equally generous and well-deserved tribute he paid to my old colleague from Quebec, now the dean of this House of Commons, for the service he was able to render to his country and to his fellow citizens during the last war as minister of national defence for air. It is refreshing to find that we have these sentiments, and that party affiliations have not prevented us from giving expression to them when there is proper occasion for doing so.
I think it was quite refreshing also to hear the tribute paid by the present member for Yale (Mr. Jones) to the nobility of character and the service rendered to the country by the former member for Yale, though they were not of the same political allegiance. I am sure that all hon. members who had the privilege of being fellow members of the late Hon. Grote Stirling were deeply gratified that there was this opportunity of paying a tribute to his memory, which we all would have been delighted to pay as soon as we learned of his death if it had not been contrary to the usual practice in this house, which is to refer only to those who are still members of parliament.
I believe there has been general agreement that there was occasion for assistance in some form in the discharge of the heavy responsibilities that now weigh upon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). There has been a suggestion that under the terms of the National Defence Act the same thing could have been done by the governor general in council without coming to parliament. Perhaps those who hold that view are right. Perhaps the present situation is as defined in the National Defence Act as an emergency, which means war, invasion, riot or insurrection, real or apprehended. We did not feel that there would be unanimity over such a construction of the present facts. If the governor in council had the right to do it without coming to parliament, it was thought parliament would not feel that it was offensive to ask parliament to state by statute, because this is to be a statute, that under present conditions one of the three authorized by the act might now be appointed.
As to the division of duties, the hon. and gallant member for Nanaimo suggests that a more clear-cut division would be the appointment of a minister for air. I have pointed out the distribution of our forces at the present time, and it is almost impossible to have separated the civil administration of these units belonging to the three different services. The arrangements that are entered into with the host countries, where there are members of our forces, are arrangements

that apply to all the members of our forces who may be there. These arrangements are very closely connected. The arrangements we make for the establishment of airfields and barracks at Grostenquin have a bearing upon like arrangements that are being discussed for barracks in Germany or barracks in Belgium. We are now fourteen allies in this North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and we are trying to adopt a pattern that will suit the purposes of all. These arrangements have to be negotiated and dealt with by one minister for the three services. I hope there will not be confusion in the performance of the work that has to be done by the minister and the associate minister.
The hon. gentleman says that the Minister of National Defence has a passion for doing it all, or for seeing to all that has any bearing upon that for which he is responsible. Well, that is no doubt a fault, in one aspect, but it is one to which I have to confess, too. But I find that in other aspects it is not altogether unfortunate that one can take details into account. After all, a nation is made up of individuals, and the implementation of policies is made up of an infinity of various small actions. The hon. member knows better than I do that the credit brought to this country by the performance of our armed forces during the last war was the result of the sum total of individual action of individual men and women, and the whole was magnificent because each small part had been regarded as important and an essential contribution to the whole picture.
I trust that there will not be such an amount of attention devoted to detail as will prevent one from seeing the forest itself as well as the trees. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) says there should be something specific for which the new minister will be responsible. The new minister, like all his colleagues, will be constitutionally responsible for everything that will have taken place in that department as well as in any other department of government. I have made no answer to the oft-repeated assertion that, in connection with the irregularities disclosed by the Currie report, each member of the government was constitutionally responsible. That is the doctrine and will continue to be the doctrine, not because I admit it but because it has come down through the traditional development of parliamentary institutions.
I hope the manner in which this will work will prove a very great alleviation of the heavy burden the present minister has to carry, and will make it humanly possible, within the twenty-four hours of each day of
National Defence Act
a man's life, to have closer supervision of all the incidents connected with the expenditure of money appropriated by parliament to perform this job. I am sure the whole Canadian public wants to see it performed, but performed as efficiently and as economically as it can be performed under the best possible supervision.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no occasion to extend the debate in committee. The bill will come before the house and it will be possible then to discuss it. I would point out, however, that nothing the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said in any way deals with what was placed before the house by the hon. member for Nanaimo, who has pointed out the need for clearly defined duties on the part of the minister to be appointed and has recommended the appointment of a minister for air. That course would be consistent with the practice in every other major country which carries on under the same system as ours or one similar to it.
In disposing of this matter at present, we leave it in the position that we will discuss it when the bill comes forward; but in view of what has been said with regard to this matter by the hon. member for Nanaimo, the hon. member for Greenwood and others, I would hope that the Prime Minister would review the situation and consider the advisability of following the course that has been suggested.
Far from a satisfactory situation prevailing there is one of confusion and great waste of public money which needs to be dealt with. That was the purpose of the suggestions that were made-as well as the welfare and efficiency of the armed forces-and which were put forward clearly, and with great understanding of their need, by those who advocated this course. The detailed discussion of this subject can take place on the bill itself, but I hope that the government will still reconsider the course they are proposing to follow.
