With deference to my hon. friend may I say that the volume of writs issued and cases tried perhaps would be an even more accurate indication of the need for a new judge. I have the figures showing the number of writs and petitions in 1942. There were 669 writs and 525 petitions, making a total of 1,194. In 1949 the writs had risen from 669 to 1,882, and the petitions from 525 to 921, for a total of 2,803 instead of 1,194. Then in 1951 the total had risen from 2,803 to 2,981. And in 1952, for only seven months-and these are the final figures for only those months, because we have to secure them from the whole of the province and there is some lag-there were a total of 3,248 writs and petitions for only seven months as compared with 1,194 for the whole twelve months as recently as 1942.
Then the figures for cases heard show that in 1942 there were 226; in 1948 there were 478; in 1951 there were 597 and for seven months of 1952 there were 440.
In 1942 there Were 5,165 motions in chambers, whereas in 1952 there were 8,195.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: What was the change in the number of judges during that period of time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
One more. My hon. friend will recall that one was added a year or so ago. So they are certainly working a lot harder than they were ten years ago, even with this new judge. Then to continue with these figures: In 1942 there were 973 undefended divorce actions; in 1949 there were 1,572; in 1951, there were 1,554 and in 1952, 1,134.
In 1942 there were 598 lawyers in the province, while in 1952 there were 1,024.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Perhaps to a lawyer the figures the minister has given would be a satisfactory answer to the suggestion that another judge be appointed. Perhaps, however, there is another answer; that prior to this time the judges really did not have much to do, and that they could deal with twice as many cases as they were dealing with before. I do not think they work a great deal of overtime-and would the minister please let me finish before he interrupts?

Judges Act
This may not be a very convincing argument, but it will be better if I have a chance to complete it at this time.
In all walks of life today-and I am not suggesting that it should be carried too far in court procedure, because that is something that should not be unduly hurried, and cannot be done on an assembly-line basis- people are doing more work in less time than they did before. If the minister would speak to a logger who worked in the British Columbia woods twenty-five years ago and to another who works in those woods today, he would find out that there is a great deal of difference in the amount of work each logger did.
I agree that there is another side to the matter, that the population of British Columbia has increased tremendously in the last few years. That would possibly be as good a reason as any as to why there is more work. But the actual figures the minister gave may mean, as I said before, that in the recent past the judges did not have much to do. Now, when there is some work to do, they should not be so insistent upon getting further help.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: The point the hon. member has raised would be a good one if I did not have an answer for it. However, we do not appoint judges merely because we are asked to do it. We have to be shown that there is a need. Among other things we ask the question as to how much work the judges are doing. The answer to that question reveals that while in 1942 the seven judges did 1,332 sitting days' work, or an average of 16 days per month each, in 1952-

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I do not think the judges would agree with you on that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: How many months a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: In 1952 the average number of sitting days per judge per month was 16; in 1952, on the basis of eight judges, it would be 26 days, or on the basis of nine judges, including the chief justice, it would be 23 days. It will be seen therefore that there has been a substantial increase in the amount of work they do.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I think the minister might make his statement a little clearer. Unless I am mistaken, when he makes reference to 16 days and 23 days he means the days on which a judge would be sitting in court. But we must remember that a judge must do his homework, write his judgments and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
The point raised by my hon. friend is quite correct. I had thought that

this would be quite obvious. The court officials have no way of keeping track of how much time a judge spends in doing his homework. They can just keep track of the time he spends in court. I was giving the sitting days only. I do not know what percentage of his time a judge would spend writing judgments and so on, but I am sure it would be substantial.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: If this bill passes, which I presume it will, is there any set date by which the appointment must be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: If this bill passes, as I hope it will, the desire will be to have the appointment made as soon as possible, because we want to get the new judge working right away.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I just wanted to point out that if the appointment is held off until after the election the services of the hon. member for Kamloops will be available.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: After the election there will be more chance of a Conservative government being in power.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I do not
believe the minister has given us the details of the arrears. I think the hon. member for Vancouver East ought to be satisfied that the judges are not actually doing six or seven times as much work as they did in 1942. If the figures are available, I think we should have the number of cases in arrears awaiting judgment. Has the minister any comparative figures relating to other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Yes, I have, but I think it would be most undesirable to give them unless an application were being made by the other provinces for the appointment of a judge. The figures I have indicate that on a comparable basis the need for an additional judge in British Columbia is substantial. I feel that will answer my hon. friend's question. I would not feel free to put the figures for another province on the record unless that province was urging the appointment of a judge.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Has the
minister the same feeling with regard to comparable figures as to cases awaiting judgment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: You mean arrears?

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I have no figures as to arrears. I understand from the fairly lengthy exchange of correspondence which took place between myself and the Chief Justice that the arrears in British Columbia are not substantial. The

judges have been working very hard in order to keep up with their work. I do not think the arrears are necessarily a good criterion because if a court is not being carefully run and if the case load is not being properly distributed, it is quite possible to build up considerable arrears when the judges available should with proper distribution be able to handle the load. I think the real test as to whether another judge is needed is the increase in the volume of work and the number of sitting days each judge puts in.
The figures I put in indicate that these judges are carrying a heavy load. They have to do a lot of homework in addition to their sitting days in court. If by hard work they have kept themselves free from an accumulation of reserved judgments, the fact remains that they still need additional help.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I do not
question the fact that most judges work very hard, but the figures given by the minister seem to leave one question in my mind. If I understood them correctly, they appear to show that the judges seem to be trying about five times as many cases as formerly. If there is any answer that can be readily given to that, I shall be interested to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Vancouver East has put his finger upon part of the explanation. The case load in 1942 may have been on the low side. Since then there has been an increase of about 40 per cent in population and the number of lawyers has nearly doubled. From being on the low side, the case load is now on the high side and an additional judge is needed to take care of a load which is heavy and still increasing. Even with an additional judge these judges will be working quite hard.

subtopic: SALARY FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE OF SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I think there is one aspect of this matter which has not been recognized by hon. members. Not only has there been a great increase in population in British Columbia, the picture has changed greatly as to distribution of population. There are now large and prosperous communities in the north and in other parts of the province far away from existing centres of population. While not a practising lawyer I know from contacts I have made that there is considerably more work for judges on circuits, more need for them to spend a great length of time away from Vancouver and Victoria. Therefore the amount of time spent by a judge in carrying out his duties would not be accounted for entirely by the number of cases on the docket.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I can only assume that there must have been some reason in the minds of the members of parliament and the authorities in drafting the original act when they restricted the officers qualified to take these affidavits to notaries public. What reason is now advanced why it should be desirable to enlarge it to include commissioners for oaths? I must say I see no objection but I am; a little curious to know what was the original reason for restricting it, and why the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the practice prevails under this statute of doing away with the retention of voluminous documents by taking microfilm reproductions of them which are properly authenticated. Having regard to the fact that the original documents are destroyed and that all that is left of documents which may be very important are these films, I would offer the theory-I do not know for sure what the reason was, but I imagine this is it-that the reason for providing that the taking of the film had to be sworn to before a notary public was that they thought that might give an oath which was a little bit more serious or solemn than if taken before a commissioner for taking oaths.
But as time went on a number of these films were sworn to before commissioners, and the result is that a lot of material in microfilm form, the authenticity of which is beyond any doubt whatever, would now be technically, in a legal sense, valueless for the purposes for which it was originally prepared. The purpose of the bill is twofold. It is to provide that these microfilms, the taking of which has been proven by oath sworn by a commissioner rather than a notary public, shall be legal retroactively, and that from now on it will be possible to authenticate microfilms of that sort before a commissioner.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Is this not a rather peculiar procedure to follow? I notice that several of the bills on the order paper contain a similar provision. They purport to amend the revised statutes of 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: The house is being asked to approve that legislation without having any idea whether or not the amendment fits into the revised statutes. Are we not a little premature in passing these different amendments to the revised statutes of 1952 when we do not even have those statutes? Why is it necessary to include these changes in the bills before we actually see the revised statutes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Well, for the reason that this bill and the revised statutes of 1952, to be completely effective for the purpose for which they were prepared, have to be a complete entity so that those referring to those statutes later on will know when they reach into the bookcase and pick out the volumes of the 1952-53 statutes and of the revised statutes of 1952 that these are the law as it stood in 1952, complete and entire. If we did not, in the course of this amendment we are putting through now, insert this part II revising the revised statutes of
1952,	then the revised statutes of 1952 when they were later proclaimed in their present form would repeal this very bill we are now passing. Thus later we shall not only have to look at the amendments passed in
1953,	1954 and 1955 and so on, but we would

have to look back to the statutes of 1952-53 and the revised statutes of 1952 to ascertain what the law was. That is why, as my hon. friend can see, we have included in all these bills a part II which merely has the effect of leaving the revised statutes of 1952 in the position in which they must be, if when they are proclaimed they are not to repeal the bill we are now passing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Will this part II appear in the actual revised statutes of 1952?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Yes, in effect.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: If the minister is right in that, it means that we cannot get the revised statutes of 1952 until the end of this session because the amendments involved in all the bills that are to go through the house during this session will have to be written into the revised statutes of 1952, will they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Well, as I was explaining a few moments ago, we cannot get them anyhow because there is this printing lag. If we could get them it would be a different question, but we cannot.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: It does seem unreal that the house should be called upon to pass this legislation without in effect being able to check it at all. Why not do as I believe has been done in the province of British Columbia? Where there is a revision as of a certain year there may also be statutes passed in that same year, and you have to look at those in order to be sure that the revised statutes have not been changed. Here we are in a new year. This is not the session of 1952. This is the session of 1952-53.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER
speechtext: The revision is supposed to be as of 1952. Should the statutes of 1952-53 not be in the ordinary form and make amendments of the law as it now stands? The lawyers will have to check that, but it seems to me there is no justification for asking the house to pass legislation of this type when we really do not know anything about it. We are not in a position to check it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT AFFIDAVIT TO BE SWORN BEFORE A NOTARY OR A COMMISSIONER

We see in part I of the bill the substance of our amendment, and all that part II of the bill says is that the substance of it will be carried into the revised statutes. That is all.
